context: An internal API serves 3 consumer teams (mobile, web dashboard, data pipeline). The API needs to change the response format for the /users endpoint: the current flat structure with 'firstName' and 'lastName' fields needs to become a nested 'name' object with 'given' and 'family' fields to support internationalization (some cultures have mononyms, others have multiple family names). All 3 consumers parse these fields. The API team has no deploy coordination authority over consumer teams — they can only communicate via Slack and shared docs. Consumer teams have varying sprint schedules and priorities.
question: How should the API team handle this breaking change: deprecation period with both formats, versioned endpoints (v1/v2), or a migration flag (consumers opt-in to new format)?
expert_answer: Versioned endpoints (v2) with a 90-day deprecation timeline for v1. The v2 endpoint returns the new nested format. v1 continues to work unchanged but includes a deprecation header. After 90 days, v1 returns 410 Gone.
expert_reasoning: Deprecation-with-both-formats (returning both flat and nested simultaneously) bloats every response and creates ambiguity about which format consumers should read — some may read both and get confused when they diverge. A migration flag requires every consumer to change their request pattern AND their parsing logic in a single coordinated deploy, which is impractical when teams have different sprint schedules. Versioned endpoints cleanly separate concerns: v1 consumers continue working with zero changes until they are ready, v2 consumers get the clean new format, and the 90-day deadline creates urgency without emergency. The API team controls the timeline unilaterally. The overhead of maintaining two endpoints for 90 days is modest since the underlying data is the same — only the serialization layer differs.
anti_pattern: A 'big bang' migration date where all consumers must update simultaneously by a specific deadline. This requires cross-team deploy coordination that the API team has no authority to enforce. When the deadline arrives, the mobile team is in a release freeze, the data pipeline team has a production incident, and the web team forgot. The API team either delays (indefinitely) or breaks consumers who missed the deadline, creating an outage.
